newsitem.title: MALDIVES: Leaders of India, Pakistan to hold first talks.
newsitem.headline: Leaders of India, Pakistan to hold first talks.

text.p: The prime ministers of India and Pakistan meet this week in the highest-level negotiations between the arch-rivals in four years, but diplomats cautioned against expectations of a quick breakthrough in the peace talks.
Pakistani Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif and his Indian counterpart, Inder Kumar Gujral, were to hold their first face-to-face talks on Monday at a resort on this Indian Ocean island nation.
The meeting will be held on the sidelines of a summit meeting of the South Asian Association for Regional Cooperation (SAARC).
Sharif was named prime minister in February and Gujral took office three weeks ago. They have exchanged letters expressing their hope that the two longtime rivals could ease tensions.
Asked after arriving at Male's airport on Sunday if he looked forward to seeing Gujral, Sharif said: "Yes, I look forward to that." Gujral made no remarks to reporters upon arriving.
Pakistani Foreign Minister Gohar Ayub Khan played down the prospects of a quick breakthrough in peace talks with
"Expectations should not be built up because unless the groundwork is there, there could be disappointments," Khan said.
Khan said it would be a drawn-out negotiation between the two nations over the divided region of Kashmir, the cause of two of the three wars they have fought since independence in 1947.
The two states launched bilateral talks in March after a three-year hiatus marked by tension over Kashmir, where officials say more than 20,000 people have died in a separatist insurgency.

The two nations' foreign secretaries -- the senior-most civil servants in the foreign ministries -- met in March, followed by talks last month between Khan and Gujral, who was foreign minister before being elevated to prime minister.
Indian and Pakistani officials said there could be agreements in a range of areas before the quarrel over Kashmir is resolved.
Khan said a settlement over Kashmir would take "a long time", but progress in other areas such as relaxing travel restrictions, boosting trade and releasing prisoners could be expected sooner.

"Once we form groups to tackle the issues, then we'll see how it is, because Kashmir naturally will take a long time," Khan said. "The other issues won't take so much time, and probably most of them would start showing results sooner than the Kashmir one."
Khan's remarks indicated that while Pakistan continued to insist that Kashmir should be on the agenda in bilateral talks, it was willing to allow progress in less contentious areas.

India welcomed Khan's stance. "That makes sense to us because that is what we have been saying, that intractable issues cannot be settled overnight," Indian Foreign Ministry spokesman Talmiz Ahmad told Reuters Television, citing Kashmir.
"I think we must move forward on the other issues that can be resolved, and I think that some of the issues that have been mentioned are ones we can make progress on."
Asked to describe Monday's meeting between Gujral and Sharif, Khan said: "It would be ice-breaking, it would give a direction to the foreign secretaries' meeting that would take place in Islamabad."
The Indian Foreign Ministry spokesman called Monday's meeting informal and said he did not expect any major announcements although the dates of foreign secretary talks could be announced.
Sharif was scheduled to leave the SAARC meeting on Tuesday, one day before its conclusion, to attend another regional summit in Turkmenistan, Pakistani diplomats said.
